The Findings in Five Lines
  1. Singapore runs much of Asia: 4,200 regional headquarters, the third-largest currency market and 61% of Southeast Asia's foreign investment.
  2. It buys about S$48B of IT services, roughly as much as India; S$31–38B of it is served by Singapore-based providers.
  3. The market is led by NCS and the global majors; Indian majors earn S$300–500M each here, most mid-tier firms under S$40M.
  4. Onshore talent is expensive: 6–8x India at entry level, 2–3.5x for seniors, and the strong S$ widens the gap.
  5. The fit for a new entrant is a small senior team on the ground, local partnerships, and junior work kept offshore.

Few economies play as crucial a role in Asia relative to their size as Singapore. A rich but relatively small economy, about 15% the size of India's, it has made itself the place from which much of the region is run: about 4,200 companies keep regional headquarters there, it is the world's third-largest currency trading centre, and it draws 61% of the foreign investment flowing into Southeast Asia. That position has held up well. The economy grew about 5% in both 2024 and 2025 and is forecast to grow 4.5–5.5% in 2026, although much of that strength comes from demand for AI-related electronics, and the IMF expects growth to settle nearer 2.5% a year. For businesses, the trade-off is a familiar one: Singapore is easy to set up in but expensive to operate in, and a central bank that is letting the S$ strengthen keeps pushing those costs up.

Its role as a hub also explains why Singapore spends so much on technology. Businesses and government there bought about S$48B of IT services in 2025, roughly as much as India, an economy almost seven times larger. About S$14B of that came directly from providers abroad, leaving a domestic market, served by Singapore-based providers, of S$31–38B. Five sectors account for 86% of purchases, and many of these buyers purchase on behalf of the whole region, even if some vendors are still chosen at a global headquarters elsewhere. The largest of them are also changing how they buy. The banks are cutting staff, building their own offshore centres and, under tighter central bank rules, scrutinising their vendors more closely, while AI is pulling spend towards data and integration work and away from labour-heavy services such as maintenance and testing.

The supply side is broad and turns over quickly. About 38,000 IT businesses are registered, and fewer than half of new firms last ten years. At the top, NCS leads, followed by the global majors, and the same names dominate government work: NCS and Accenture won 41% of it, and access runs through supplier panels. Indian firms themselves are split. The majors earn S$300–500M each in Singapore, while most mid-tier firms earn under S$40M. Across the market, offshore delivery is the norm rather than the exception; even NCS, a local champion, delivers from centres in India, China, Vietnam and the Philippines.

Talent is where an onshore presence becomes expensive. A Singapore IT professional costs about 6x to 8x an Indian one at entry level, a gap that narrows to 2x to 3.5x for senior staff, and the stronger S$ has added 42% to the rupee cost of a Singapore salary since 2019. The gap is smallest in the skills Singapore lacks most, such as AI, data, cloud and cybersecurity. Bringing people in from abroad does not close it either: foreign professionals must be paid a minimum salary close to what a local graduate earns, and once a firm has 25 professionals, the rules start to weigh its nationality mix.

Taken together, the findings point a new entrant towards a small, senior team on the ground, with client-facing roles hired locally, delivery leads transferred from India and mainstream junior work kept offshore. Juniors who do need to be onshore are best hired locally: that improves the firm's nationality mix, which the local policy rewards. Reaching the largest buyers will take patience, and local strategic partnerships, as banks and government buy through supplier panels and vendor checks. Two risks hang over this picture: a pullback in AI spending could slow growth, and a strengthening S$ would keep raising the cost of every onshore hire in rupee terms.

The report is organised in four parts. Part 1 sets out Singapore's economic outlook, its role as Asia's business hub, and the trends that will shape demand. Part 2 sizes the market and identifies the sectors and organisations that buy. Part 3 turns to the sellers: who they are, how government work is won, how Indian firms have fared and which firms could serve as delivery partners. Part 4 follows the talent: where it comes from, which skills are short, what it costs against India and how the hiring rules work. Appendix A sets out the scope and conventions, and Appendix B explains how each figure was built.

This report was prepared to help Wissen Technology understand the Singapore IT services market and to inform its business development plans and strategy. It is fact-based research that draws from publicly available information.

Part 1

Macro Context and Outlook

How large and fast-growing Singapore's economy is, what it is made of, why so much of Asia's business is run from it, and what it costs to operate there.

In brief
  1. About 15% the size of India's economy, yet it draws 61% of the foreign investment into Southeast Asia.
  2. Growth of about 5% in 2024 and 2025 rests on AI electronics; the IMF expects it to settle near 2.5% a year.
  3. Easy to set up in, expensive to run in, and the S$ is set to keep strengthening.

Singapore: The Gateway to Southeast Asia

Singapore is where much of Asia's business is run from, which is why its IT services market is larger than its economy alone would suggest.M1.6

61%

Singapore's share of foreign direct investment into Southeast Asia in 2025; about 4,200 multinationals run regional headquarters here.M1.6

Regional headquarters, banks, fund managers, traders and shipping firms manage the region from here, and many of their regional IT budgets sit here too. Singapore plays some key roles in the world economy, and each brings its own IT demand:

The Asia HQ
About 4,200 regional headquarters, roughly 3x Hong Kong's count

New investment keeps coming: headquarters and professional services made up 62% of the business spending secured in 2025 by the Economic Development Board (EDB), the government agency that attracts foreign investment. These firms run systems for several countries from here.M1.6

IT demand: multi-country ERP, shared services, regional platforms

A global financial centre
Third-largest currency trading centre, 11.8% of global trading

Its fund managers hold S$6.7 trillion, 76% of it from investors outside Singapore. This drives demand for trading, payments and wealth-management systems.M1.6

IT demand: trading, payments, wealth management

A trade and logistics hub
A record 44.7 million containers through the port in 2025

Most goods leaving Singapore pass through rather than being made here. The buyers are port, airport and shipping operators and the logistics firms around them, such as PSA International, Changi Airport Group and SATS (Part 2). They need systems that track cargo, schedule ships and flights, and clear customs across several countries.M1.6

IT demand: cargo tracking, scheduling, customs

For IT services, a buyer in Singapore often buys for the whole region. But the budget and the choice of vendor are not always in the same place: a regional headquarters may fund a project while its global headquarters in the US, Europe or China picks the vendor.M1.6

Business Environment

Singapore is easy to operate in, but expensive at the same time.

Easy to set up

Singapore is the only Southeast Asian economy the World Bank rates as business-ready, and corporate tax is 17%.M1.7

Expensive to operate

Grade A office space in the business district costs about S$12 (≈Rs 880) per square foot a month, and rents are rising as AI firms expand. The cost of an onshore presence is going up.M1.7

Outlook and Key Themes, 2026 and Beyond

Growth is running well above its usual pace and is expected to settle back.M1.8

4.5–5.5%

METI's 2026 growth forecast, lifted by AI hardware spending; the IMF expects about 2.5% a year from 2028.M1.8

The economy grew about 3.6% a year on average in 2020–2025, but about 5% in each of 2024 and 2025. METI forecasts 4.5–5.5% for 2026, lifted by global spending on AI hardware; the IMF expects about 3% in 2027 and 2.5% a year after that. The government's long-term plan, the Economic Strategy Review (June 2026), bets on deploying AI across the economy, deepening the finance and headquarters hub, and helping an ageing workforce adapt.M1.8

The central bank (MAS) manages the Singapore dollar, and it is set to keep strengthening. For a firm that earns in rupees, onshore staff in Singapore cost more each year, while work delivered from India gets cheaper for Singapore clients.M1.7

Six themes will shape demand. Tailwinds first, then headwinds; each opens as you scroll to it. The IT column is our judgement, not a measured effect.M1.8

Interactive · scroll to open each theme in turn, or click one
Tailwind
Ageing and a tight labour market
What is happening
More than a fifth of citizens are 65 or older; women have 0.87 children on average; workforce growth depends on foreign workers.
What it means for Singapore
Firms must do more with fewer local workers.
What it means for IT services
More automation and outsourcing; more acceptance of offshore delivery where rules allow.
Tailwind
Finance and headquarters hub deepening
What is happening
The government wants Singapore to run, fund and regulate business across the region, not just host offices; money managed by fund managers grew 10% in 2025.
What it means for Singapore
Finance stays at about 14% of the economy.
What it means for IT services
The largest IT-buying sector keeps growing; regulation adds resilience and compliance work.
Headwind, near term
US tariffs and trade fragmentation
What is happening
Firms rushed exports out in 2025 before US tariffs took effect; the IMF sees rising trade barriers as a key risk.
What it means for Singapore
Trade and manufacturing, 39% of the economy, take the hit.
What it means for IT services
Trade and manufacturing firms delay discretionary IT; some supply-chain re-planning work.
Small headwind
Middle East conflict and energy prices
What is happening
Energy prices rose in 2026; the central bank twice let the S$ rise faster to hold down prices; the carbon tax rose to S$45 a tonne.
What it means for Singapore
Higher costs for firms that use a lot of energy; a stronger S$.
What it means for IT services
Cost pressure on transport, chemicals and logistics buyers; a stronger S$ helps offshore pricing.
Mixed: the biggest shift
AI investment and adoption
What is happening
Global spending on AI chips and servers lifted Singapore's 2026 growth forecast. The government plans to use AI across the economy, not build its own AI models.
What it means for Singapore
Growth leans heavily on the AI boom; if AI spending falls, growth falls with it.
What it means for IT services
More work integrating AI, data and governance into existing systems; AI also squeezes labour-heavy work such as maintenance and testing, and its pricing.
Watch
Global minimum tax
What is happening
Since 2025, large multinationals pay at least 15% tax wherever they operate.
What it means for Singapore
Tax breaks become a weaker reason for companies to base their regional headquarters here.
What it means for IT services
Fewer new regional headquarters would mean fewer new buyers; no sign yet (headquarters still 62% of new business spending in 2025).

Part 2

Market Overview: The Buy Side

How much Singapore's businesses and government spend on IT services, how much of it goes to Singapore-based providers, and which sectors and organisations do the buying.

In brief
  1. Buyers spent about S$48B in 2025; S$14B went straight to providers abroad, leaving a domestic market of S$31–38B, about 4–5% of GDP.
  2. Five sectors make 86% of purchases; government and media buy far above their size, manufacturing far below.
  3. Banks are cutting staff, building their own offshore centres and checking vendors harder.

Market Size

Singapore businesses and government spent about S$48B on IT services in 2025. About S$14B was bought directly from providers abroad, and the IT services bought domestically are estimated at S$31–38 billion, about 4–5% of GDP.M2.1 M2.6

Government and media buy far above their size. Government buys 16% of IT services from 2% of output, and media and telecom 13% from 3%. Estimates differ, and part of the gap may be a statistical artefact.M2.6

Manufacturing is 19% of national output but makes about 1% of IT services purchases. The reason is not clear from the data. It may be the capital-heavy nature of the sector, or that global manufacturers buy IT centrally for the whole group, which their Singapore entities use without buying it here.M2.6

Buyer Trends

The largest buying sector, finance, is changing how it buys IT services.M3.9

Headcount
Banks are cutting staff and leaning on AI

DBS, OCBC and UOB had about 2,800 fewer employees at end-2025 than a year earlier. DBS said in February 2025 it would shed about 4,000 temporary and contract roles over three years as AI takes on more work.M3.9

In-house centres
Banks run their own offshore technology centres

DBS Tech India in Hyderabad had over 3,000 staff by 2022. These in-house centres are the main substitute for IT services firms (Part 3).M3.9

Regulation
The regulator is pushing resilience and tighter control of vendors

MAS penalised DBS in 2023 after repeated outages, a signal to all banks to invest in system stability. Since December 2024, binding MAS rules require banks to keep audit rights over their IT vendors, including offshore delivery centres. Offshore delivery to banks remains allowed, but each bank deal now carries heavier due diligence. NCS names "digital resilience" as a growth driver.M3.9

Beyond the Headline

Tech firms also bought S$33.7B of IT services from each other in 2023. This has been left out because most of it double counts the same spend, through subcontracting, resale and other charges.M2.7

Part 3

Competitive Landscape: Service Providers

What Singapore's IT firms earn and from whom, how the market is structured, who the main competitors are, how government work is won, and which firms could be delivery partners.

In brief
  1. A crowded market led by NCS and global majors such as Accenture, NTT DATA, IBM and TCS.M3.2 M3.5
  2. Indian firms are split: majors earn S$300–500M each here, most mid-tier firms under S$40M.
  3. Government work is concentrated and runs through supplier panels; offshore delivery is the norm, even for NCS.

How Much Singapore IT Firms Earn

Singapore's IT firms earned an estimated S$69B in 2025, and about half of it came from clients outside Singapore.M2.2 M2.3

Singapore is a regional hub: much of what its IT industry produces is sold to the rest of the region. Revenue grew about 15–20% a year from 2019 to 2024M2.8; the wider information and communications sector grew about 10% in 2025.M2.5 New IT company registrations rose 15% in 2025 and are rising faster in 2026.M3.1M3.7

About half of what Singapore IT firms earn comes from abroad

Singapore's total IT services spend is roughly the same size as India's. The big difference is exports: India's IT industry exports about 78% of what it earns, against 46–55% for Singapore's, so India's industry is about 3x larger.M3.7

Market Structure

The market is crowded and fragmented. About 38,000 IT businesses are registered, most of them small.M3.1

Buyers have many options, so a newcomer stands out only through a clear specialism; the many small local firms are also potential partners or subcontractors. Only one firm publishes a clear lead: NCS, Singtel's IT services arm, is ranked first in Singapore by vendor revenue.M3.5

We group competitors into five segments, set by their size and delivery model. Segments 1 and 2 lead on large programmes; segments 3, 4 and 5 compete for narrower work. In-house technology teams at banks and in government are the main substitute. Offshore delivery is the norm, even for the local champion: NCS delivers from Pune, Chengdu, Hanoi and Manila, including some Singapore government work from Hanoi.M3.5 M3.9

Coforge is the exception in the mid-tier: its Singapore company nearly doubled to S$38M. TCS's 1,000-seat banking and financial services centre in Singapore, opened in 2015, remains the clearest benchmark for the onshore scale a large Indian firm runs for Singapore banks.M3.9

These Indian firms' Singapore subsidiaries together earn about S$900M, but this understates Singapore market revenue.M3.3 M3.4 Firms define geography and scope differently: some Singapore entities also serve other countries in the region or count non-services revenue, while major firms (such as Infosys, Wipro, Tech Mahindra, LTM) run their main Singapore business through branches or bill it from India.

Government Work

Government buys 16% of IT services, and its work is concentrated: NCS and Accenture won S$1.6B, or 41%, of the S$4.0B of government IT services awards in FY21–FY25, and the top ten won 65%. Indian firms won about 4%, mostly application maintenance.M2.6 M3.6

Entry runs through GovTech's supplier panels; the August 2025 panel has 57 firms, including TCS, HCLTech, Wipro, Tech Mahindra and Infosys Compaz. MAS keeps a separate 30-firm panel for its own IT work, which includes several small Indian-origin firms. Some government work is delivered offshore, but providers must meet the government's IT security rules, and agencies may require data to stay in Singapore depending on its sensitivity.M3.6

Select Profiles

Six firms publish enough to profile: two local or global leaders, three Indian majors and one offshore-led mid-tier firm.

Figures are for each firm's Singapore companies unless stated.

NCS
Segment 2 · Singapore

Singapore's largest IT services firm by vendor revenue.M3.5 Owned by Singtel; also operates in Australia, Greater China and Southeast Asia. Group revenue was S$3.2B in the year to March 2026, up 7%, with record bookings of S$3.8B. Organised around government (Gov+), telecom (Telco+) and enterprise clients. Won 22% of government IT services award value in FY21–FY25.M3.6

Accenture
Segment 1 · Ireland

The largest global major in Singapore's public-sector IT work. Won 19% of government IT services award value in FY21–FY25, including a S$109M business registry system.M3.6 Opened an AI engineering hub in Singapore in 2024.M3.2

TCS
Segment 1 · India

Its Singapore company earned S$490M in FY2026. The company is a regional hub: it also owns subsidiaries elsewhere in Asia, so the revenue figure includes non-Singapore clients. It sits on GovTech's main IT panel.M3.6

Infosys
Segment 1 · India

Runs three Singapore vehicles. Infosys Compaz, 60% owned with Temasek since 2018, earned S$94M; Infosys Singapore, a regional consulting company, earned S$45M. They also sit on GovTech's main IT panel.M3.6

HCLTech
Segment 1 · India

HCL Singapore earned S$345M in the year to March 2026, up 4%; revenue from Singapore customers rose 12% to S$299M.M3.3 Staff costs were S$150M, which points to a large local workforce. Revenue includes hardware and software licence resale.

Coforge
Segment 3 · India

Offshore-led firm with a fast-growing Singapore company. Coforge Pte Ltd's revenue nearly doubled to S$38M in the year to March 2026.M3.3 Local staff costs were flat at S$5.7M, so the growth was likely delivered through offshore or other channels.

Potential Delivery Partners

Three firms that could serve as delivery partners.M3.8

Ufinity
Local mid-sized firm, Singapore

A Singapore software and digital services firm; Ufinity Group was registered in 2010.M3.8 It works mainly for government: it won S$46M of government IT services awards in FY21–FY25, including S$40M to develop and maintain the Ministry of Education's Student Learning Space, and sits on GovTech's agile development panels.M3.6 M3.8

It also offers custom development, application migration and testing.

Part 4

Talent Ecosystem

Where tech talent comes from, which roles are short, what it costs, how long it stays, how firms hire, and the role of policy and regulation.

In brief
  1. Most of Singapore's 222,200 tech professionals work for buyers, so an IT firm competes for people with its own clients.
  2. Singapore pay is 6–8x India at entry level and 2–3.5x for seniors; the S$ alone added 42% since 2019.
  3. Foreign hires must be paid near local graduate rates, and past 25 professionals the nationality mix starts to count.

Talent Supply and Pipelines

222,200

tech professionals in Singapore in 2025, up 3.8% in a year; 59% of them work outside the IT industry, mostly in banks and other enterprises.M4.1

Where Singapore's tech professionals work, 2025
41%about 91,000 people
Inside the IT industry
59%about 131,000 people
Outside the IT industry

The 59% work for banks, insurers, manufacturers and other enterprises: the same organisations an IT services firm sells to.

An IT services firm competes for people with its own clients.M4.1

New talent arrives through three pipelines. Computing graduates start at a median of S$5,500 to S$6,400 a month, which is close to the minimum salary for a foreign professional (S$5,600 a month), a link that matters for the regulations below.M4.1

Universities
Six publicly funded universities award most computing degrees

NUS and NTU run the largest computing schools; SMU combines business and technology; SIT is applied and industry-linked; SUTD is design- and engineering-led; SUSS serves part-time and adult learners.

Polytechnics and ITE
Five polytechnics offer IT diplomas

Singapore, Ngee Ann, Temasek, Nanyang and Republic polytechnics offer IT diplomas, and the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) trains technicians.

Foreign professionals
201,200 Employment Pass holders, about 12% of professional jobs

In information and communications, foreign pass holders fill up to a quarter of professional roles, against under 15% in finance. Who can be hired this way is set by the regulations below.

Roles in Demand and in Shortage

Demand has narrowed to specialists. AI, data, cybersecurity and cloud roles are in short supply, while hiring for generalist roles has become selective.M4.9

16.7%

of Singapore tech job postings asked for at least one AI skill in 2025, up from 14% in 2024.M4.9

The government's shortage list, which gives foreign hires in these roles extra Employment Pass points, has carried the same core tech roles since it began in 2023.M4.9

AI and data
AI engineer, AI researcher, data scientist, data engineer

MOM names data scientists and AI engineers among the drivers of professional hiring; postings asking for two or more AI skills rose from 4.9% to 7.6% (2024 to 2025).

Software
Software developer, applications and systems programmer, web and mobile developer, software development manager

Among the top professional vacancies in 2024 and 2025, and still among the hardest to fill.

Cloud and security
Cloud specialist, cybersecurity architect, penetration tester, digital forensics specialist

Recruiters' main hiring areas alongside AI; expected 2026 pay rises of up to 18%, against 6% to 10% for tech overall.

How demand is shifting

Four signals from 2024 to 2025M4.9
Tech employment growth, 2025

Led by finance, professional services and manufacturing

Vacancies unfilled for 6+ months

Rising again after three years of improvement

Vacancies to be filled from overseas

Employers planning fewer foreign hires

Vacancies that can be done remotely

Remote work is growing, mainly in mainstream roles

Recruiters describe tech hiring as more selective, with momentum in applied AI, data engineering and cybersecurity, and more project-based and contract hiring. The roles in shortage are specialist and senior roles, where the pay gap with India is smaller: 2x to 3.5x for senior staff, and lower for junior data and AI roles than for junior software roles. The shortage list also eases Employment Passes for them. Mainstream development is still in demand, but it is where the gap is largest and where remote work is growing.M4.9

What Talent Costs: Singapore vs India

A Singapore IT professional costs about 6x to 8x an Indian one at entry level, narrowing to 2x to 3.5x for senior staff, in nominal terms.M4.3

7–8x

a Singapore computing graduate's starting pay against an Indian campus hire: S$5,500–6,400 a month (Rs 48–56 lakh a year) against about Rs 6.8 lakh a year.M4.3

The median resident tech worker earns S$8,000 a month, against S$5,000 for all resident workers.M4.1

a) By Experience Level

The cost multiple falls from about 6x for junior staff to 2x to 3.5x for senior staff, because Singapore's pay curve is flatter: an Indian engineering manager earns about 8x a junior engineer, a Singapore one about 2.5x.M4.3

How the Gap Has Moved Since 2019

+42%

rise in the rupee cost of the same Singapore salary since 2019, from the exchange rate alone.M4.8

Rupees per Singapore dollar

The same S$ salary costs 42% more in rupees

Pay growth, 2017–2024

About the same pace: the currency drove the gap

Sources: MAS via SingStat, US Federal Reserve, MOM, PLFSM4.8Pay measures differ and are not IT-specific

The S$ has risen 42% against the rupee since 2019, so the same Singapore salary now costs 42% more in rupees. Singapore's median pay has also risen 27% since 2019. Over 2017 to 2024, the period with comparable Indian data, pay grew at about the same pace in both countries: 30% in Singapore and 28% in India. The gap has widened mainly because of the currency, and the central bank is set to keep the S$ strengthening.M4.8

Market Dynamism and Attrition

About 17% of Singapore's IT employees resign in a year, against about 14% voluntary attrition in Indian IT services. Layoffs are rarer in Singapore.M4.4

Singapore staff leave more often; Indian staff are let go more often

About 1% of resident professionals were retrenched in 2025, against about 4% employer-initiated attrition across Indian companies in 2026. Singapore professionals move for pay: 43% of those who changed jobs in 2025 got raises above 10%, and 43% plan to change roles in 2026.M4.4

Common Hiring Norms and Practices

Three norms shape how IT firms hire in Singapore.M4.5

Speed
Local hiring is fast; foreign hiring is slow

A local hire takes 2 to 4 weeks. A foreign hire adds 3 to 8 weeks for the work pass, plus a 14-day job advertisement unless exempt.

Contracts
Contract staff fill projects

Banks and large firms keep permanent teams for core and control functions and bring in contract staff for transformation, system migration, cybersecurity, and data and AI work. This is the demand that staff augmentation serves.

Terms
Other terms follow common norms

Probation of 3 to 6 months, short notice periods and a 13th-month year-end bonus are set by contract and custom rather than law.

Foreign Hiring Regulations and Incentives

Singapore's foreign hiring rules are strict but predictable: they bite hardest on junior hires and on firms with 25 or more professional staff.M4.6

A foreign professional needs an Employment Pass (EP), which has two gates. The first is a minimum salary. The second is COMPASS, a points test introduced in 2023. Its purpose is to admit foreigners who complement local workers rather than replace them, and it does this by scoring both the person and the employer. An application needs 40 points.M4.6

Key regulations and incentives for an IT services employer

RuleWhat it means for the business
Minimum salary for foreign professionalsForeign hires must be paid Singapore rates: at least S$5,600 to S$10,700 a month depending on age, rising in 2027. Bringing people onshore removes most of the India cost advantage.
Nationality mix (COMPASS)Once a firm has 25 or more professionals, a team dominated by one nationality makes each further hire of that nationality harder to approve. An India-heavy team hits a ceiling.
Shortage skillsAI, data, cloud, cybersecurity and software engineering roles get extra credit. Specialists are easier to bring in than generalists.
Intra-company transfersManagers and specialists with at least a year at the India entity can be moved for up to five years, skipping the points test and the 14-day local job advertisement; the minimum salary still applies. The quickest route for senior staff, but closed to fresh hires.
Junior foreign hires (S Pass)Allowed, but capped by local headcount and charged a S$650 monthly levy per head. Not a scalable source of juniors.
Local hiring costs and subsidiesEmployers pay up to 17% on top of a local hire's salary in retirement contributions, which they do not pay for foreigners. Government programmes can cover up to 70% of a new local hire's salary during training.
Source: MOM rules and factsheetsM4.6

Proposed Staffing Model

Cost differences and hiring rules together decide where each hire should come from.M4.7

Local hire in Singapore
Client-facing sales roles

Work is won through relationships and supplier panels (Parts 2 and 3); a local senior brings buyer networks a transferee lacks.

Junior roles that must be onshore

Little cost benefit in transferring juniors from India because of minimum salary rules. Hiring locally earns a government subsidy of up to 70% of salary during training.

Transfer from India
Delivery leads and specialists

They know the delivery model and the offshore teams, and intra-firm transfers skip the points test and job advertising.

Offshore in India
Mainstream junior delivery

A local graduate costs 7x to 8x an Indian campus hire; a junior posted to Singapore must be paid local rates anyway.

Bottom Line: Optimal Sourcing Mix
  1. Keep the onshore team small, while mainstream junior work remains in India.
  2. Once the entity passes 25 professionals, local hiring and nationality mix shape work pass decisions. Local hiring for junior roles is a cost-efficient way to improve the mix.
  3. Budget for churn: roughly one in six local staff resign every year, so replacement hiring is a standing cost.M4.4

Appendix

Scope, Method and Sources

Appendix A: Scope and Conventions

The market sized here is what Singapore-registered businesses and government pay Singapore-registered IT services providers. Regional headquarters buying for other countries count as Singapore buyers.

  • In scope: IT consulting, application development and maintenance, systems integration, cloud and infrastructure managed services, data and AI services, testing, cybersecurity services and staff augmentation.
  • Out of scope: hardware, software licences and SaaS, telecom services, business process outsourcing, IT contractors placed by staffing agencies, household spending, and purchases between tech firms.
  • Currency: S$ throughout. Current figures use January–September 2026 averages: US$1 = S$1.278 = Rs 93.92, so S$1 = Rs 73.49 (US Federal Reserve). Past figures use each year's average (MAS via SingStat).
  • Comparisons are nominal, with no adjustment for purchasing power. The base year is 2025; "(est.)" marks forecasts.
  • Sources are free and public: no paid databases and no interviews. Official statistics and regulators come first, then company filings, then analysts and the press.

Appendix B: How the Figures Were Built

Each M tag in the text links to one entry below: what the figure is, how it was built, the main caveat, and the sources.

Part 1

M1.1Growth. Yearly real growth is from SingStat's GDP series. The 2026 range is the trade ministry's August 2026 forecast, and the quarterly figures are from the 14 October 2026 advance estimate. The ministry was called MTI until it became METI on 1 October 2026. Its next forecast revision comes with the Economic Survey in November 2026.
Sources: SingStat real GDP, August 2026 forecast, third-quarter advance estimate, renaming, IMF (India).
M1.2Size and income. Nominal GDP of S$789.5B in 2025, converted at the 2025 average rate. Income per head and the India comparison use IMF data.
Sources: SingStat GDP, Economic Survey 2025, IMF.
M1.3Population and ageing. From Population in Brief 2026, as reported in the press, and SingStat's Population Trends.
Sources: Bernama, SingStat.
M1.4Other indicators. Inflation, jobs and reserves are from the Economic Survey; the inflation forecast and policy moves from MAS; credit ratings from an aggregator.
Sources: Economic Survey 2025, MAS July 2026, MAS October 2026, ratings.
M1.5Economy mix. Each sector's share of output in 2019 and 2025, grouped into the same buying sectors as Part 2.
Sources: SingStat GDP by industry, Economic Survey 2025.
M1.6Regional hub. Headquarters counts come from the press and define headquarters differently by city, so the Hong Kong comparison is indicative. Singapore's investment inflows are inflated by holding companies that pass money on to the region.
Sources: headquarters, currency trading, assets managed, Economic Survey 2025, investment flows.
M1.7Business environment. Sources: World Bank B-READY, tax, office rents, MAS July 2026, MAS October 2026.
M1.8Outlook and themes. Forecasts are from the trade ministry and the IMF. The long-term plan is from a law firm's summary of the Economic Strategy Review. The "What it means for IT services" column is our judgement.
Sources: ministry forecast, IMF data, IMF Article IV, Economic Strategy Review.

Part 2

M2.1Market size: S$31–38B (2025). Two independent methods agree. From the seller side, Singapore IT firms' revenue less exports gives S$31–38B. From the buyer side, the official input-output tables show S$33B bought from Singapore providers. An analyst estimate of S$39B (Mordor Intelligence) sits just above and does not set the range because its method is undisclosed. Caveat: the seller-side figure includes some resale and pass-through revenue.
Sources: SingStat services survey, input-output table, Mordor Intelligence.
M2.2Exports: about half. No IT-only export rate is published, so the range runs from 46% (the whole information and communications industry, 2024) to 55% (IT and information services, 2023).
Sources: services exports, input-output table, industry revenue.
M2.3IT firms' revenue: about S$69B (2025). 2024 revenue of S$63B grown at the 2025 sector rate.
Source: SingStat services survey.
M2.5Growth to 2025. 10.8% for 2024 (actual IT revenue) and 9.8% for 2025 (information and communications output); the 2025 rate may overstate IT services.
Sources: SingStat services survey, SingStat GDP by industry.
M2.6Who buys. Each sector's share of IT services purchases in the 2023 input-output tables, applied to the 2025 market; imports come from the matching import table. Caveat: government and media and telecom are likely overstated, because the official category includes hosting and the government figure includes allocated software investment.
Sources: domestic use table, import use table, GovTech ICT procurement.
M2.7Purchases between tech firms. S$33.7B in 2023, left out because most of it is subcontracting already counted at the end client; public data cannot separate the rest.
Source: domestic use table.
M2.8IT firms' growth. SingStat's survey of IT firms: 15–20% a year over 2019–2024, depending on whether computer programming is included, since that category carries large technology firms' pass-through revenue. Margins are not used because transfer pricing distorts them.
Sources: SingStat services survey, Services Sector 2024.
M2.10Notable buyers. Chosen by the size of their Singapore operations, not ranked by IT spend, which no public source reports. Recheck names before external use.

Part 3

M3.1Company register and new entrants. ACRA's register as at 16 September 2026, filtered to IT activity codes. It counts legal entities, not trading firms.
Source: ACRA.
M3.2Competitor list. Twenty-nine firms chosen by judgement, each with a live Singapore entity and at least one public sign of activity there (published revenue, a government award or panel seat, or a dated announcement).
Sources: ACRA, Accenture, Persistent, Synechron.
M3.3Singapore company revenue. From the Indian parents' annual reports (subsidiary statements) and the Singapore companies' own accounts. Some include regional revenue or hardware and licence resale; firms that operate through branches or bill from India do not appear.
Sources: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Coforge, Mphasis, Persistent, Hexaware.
M3.4Indian firms in total. The Reserve Bank of India's survey of Indian firms' foreign affiliates puts Singapore at about S$0.9B.
Source: RBI.
M3.5NCS. The ranking is IDC's, as cited by NCS and Singtel; revenue and bookings are from Singtel's results.
Sources: Singtel results, Singtel Investor Day 2026.
M3.6Government work. Government awards from April 2021 to March 2026, classed as IT services by keyword and checked by hand for the largest. Only prime contracts appear, and values often span several years. Provider rules are from GovTech and the digital ministry; vendor claims of approved offshore delivery centres were not used without a primary source.
Sources: GeBIZ awards, GovTech, MDDI.
M3.7Singapore vs India. Singapore buyers spend about S$48B on IT services, imports included, against about S$42B in India (Gartner). Definitions differ, so the ratio sits anywhere from 114% to 130%, which the body calls roughly the same size. India's industry revenue and export share are NASSCOM estimates.
Sources: Singapore input-output tables, Gartner, NASSCOM.
M3.8Delivery partners. Profiles draw on registry, procurement and company sources; none publishes Singapore revenue.
Sources: Ufinity, IFIS, IFIS staff and clients, GienTech, GienTech history, Pactera.
M3.9Market trends (Parts 2 and 3). Selected by judgement as moves that set a pattern, mainly 2024–2026.
Sources: bank headcount, DBS Tech India, MAS action on DBS, DBS IT pause, MAS outsourcing rules, Reed Smith, Baker McKenzie, NCS delivery centres, TCS centre.

Part 4

M4.1Talent supply. Workforce size and tech pay are from IMDA's Digital Economy Report as reported in the press; graduate pay from the 2025 Graduate Employment Survey; Employment Pass counts and foreign shares from MOM figures as reported in the press.
Sources: IMDA, NUS Computing, NTU survey, all universities, Employment Passes, foreign shares, resident professionals, mid-career conversion.
M4.2Pay by skill. Glassdoor India-wide market pay by job title and level in both countries, at Rs 73.49 per S$, matched by title ladder (base title as junior, Senior as mid). Used for skills because the firm's pay bands do not separate data and AI roles. Self-reported and volatile, so read the pattern, not single multiples.
Sources: Glassdoor Singapore, Glassdoor India.
M4.3Pay by level and for graduates. India: Wissen Technology's median total pay by level as reported on Levels.fyi, confirmed as broadly right by Wissen and marked down 15% to reflect the wider industry. The software engineer ladder rests on 76 submissions; solution architect, business analyst and manager on fewer than five each. The campus rate is Wissen's Rs 8 lakh, also less 15%. Singapore: Glassdoor's title ladder, using the midpoint of the middle half of reported pay (base title as junior, Senior as mid, Manager as senior); solution architect uses Glassdoor's average. Levels are matched approximately across the two sources.
Sources: Levels.fyi, Wissen Technology, Glassdoor Singapore, NUS Computing, NTU survey.
M4.4Attrition. Singapore: MOM's monthly resignation rate for IT, times 12. India: Aon's IT services attrition less the all-industry layoff rate, cross-checked against TCS and Infosys. Approximate: compare the order of magnitude.
Sources: MOM resignations, retrenchment, Aon, TCS, Infosys, job switching.
M4.5Hiring practices. Employer guides and recruiter reports.

M4.6Regulations and incentives. MOM rules and factsheets, summarised for business readers, not as legal advice.

M4.7Staffing by role. A judgement drawn from the pay gaps and hiring rules, not Wissen's plan. That local seniors bring stronger buyer networks has no cited source.
M4.8Change since 2019. Currency: Rs 51.6 per S$ in 2019 (annual average) against Rs 73.5 in January–September 2026. Pay: MOM's median full-time resident income for Singapore and PLFS average salaried earnings for India. The two measures differ and neither is IT-specific, so read the direction, not the decimals.
Sources: annual exchange rates, MOM income, PLFS via PIB.
M4.9Roles in demand and in shortage. Shortage roles are from MOM's Shortage Occupation List, which applies from 1 January 2026, grouped as in an immigration adviser's summary; the 2023 list shows the starting set. Vacancy trends are from MOM's Job Vacancies 2025 report; the AI-skill share and sector growth from IMDA's Digital Economy Report as reported in the press; hiring and pay trends from Hays and Michael Page. Recruiter views are opinion, not measurement.
